questions.question: An administrator new to ServiceNow is relating database terms to the platform. How do records and fields map onto a table?

options.text: Each record is a column and each field is a row
Each record is a row and each field is a column
Each record is a table and each field is a row
Each record is a column and each field is a table

explanation.correct: A table is a collection of records in the database. Each record corresponds to a row in the table, and each field on a record corresponds to a column on that table. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/table-administration-and-data-management/c_TableAdministration.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: This reverses the model: records are rows and fields are columns, not the other way around.
A table is the collection of records; a record is one row in it, and each field is a column.
A record corresponds to a row, and a field corresponds to a column on the table, not to a table of its own.

source.excerpt: In ServiceNow, data is organized in a database with tables, records, fields, and values.

questions.question: An administrator troubleshooting an integration needs the sys_id of an incident that is open in the form view, and does not want to write a script. What should they do?

options.text: Copy the value shown in the record's Number field
Use Copy URL from the header and read the sys_id= value
Add the Sys ID field to the form layout and copy it
Open the table's Dictionary entry and copy the record ID

explanation.correct: Every record is identified by a sys_id, a unique 32-character GUID. The docs explain that you can get it without scripting by right-clicking the form header bar, selecting Copy URL, and reading the value that follows the sys_id= parameter in the copied URL. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/c_UniqueRecordIdentifier.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The Number field is a readable record number such as INC0010001, not the 32-character GUID that the platform uses as the sys_id.
The docs state that the sys_id is not meant to appear as a field on a form or a column in a list, so adding it to the layout is not the supported way.
Dictionary entries define tables and their fields (columns); they do not hold the sys_id of an individual incident record.

source.excerpt: Records have a unique 32-character ID called a sys_id.

questions.question: An incident shows a person's name in the Caller field, which is a reference to the User [sys_user] table. With default settings, what does the field store in the database?

options.text: The caller's name, copied from the user record
The sys_id of the referenced user record
A full copy of the referenced user record
The URL of the referenced user record

explanation.correct: Each reference field stores a sys_id for each referenced record in the database, but the sys_id is not shown; the field shows the display value instead (here, the user's name). Defining a reference field creates a relationship between the two tables and makes the referenced table's fields available to the form. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/c_ReferenceField.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The name is the display value the reference field shows. The value stored in the database is the referenced record's sys_id.
A reference field does not copy the record. It stores the sys_id and makes the other fields of the referenced table available to the form.
The sys_id can be read from a record URL, but the reference field itself stores the sys_id, not a URL.

source.excerpt: A reference field stores the unique sys_id of a record from another table, creating a link between them.

questions.question: An administrator creates a new table that extends the Task [task] table to track facilities work. What should they expect for the new table?

options.text: It receives a copy of every existing Task record
It inherits the Task fields and can add fields of its own
The Task table gains every field added to the new table
Its records are stored in a database table apart from Task

explanation.correct: A table that extends another becomes a child class. Task uses the table per hierarchy model, where child classes derive their fields from the parent (Incident derives fields from Task) and each child only has Dictionary entries for the fields unique to it. So the new table gets the Task fields plus any fields it adds. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/table-administration-and-data-management/table-extension-and-classes.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Extending a table does not copy existing parent records into the child. With table per hierarchy the parent class stores all records belonging to the hierarchy.
Inheritance flows from parent to child. Fields added to the child are Dictionary entries unique to that child class and are not added to Task.
Under the table per hierarchy model used by Task, child classes do not get separate database tables; one parent database table stores the records.

source.excerpt: An extended table inherits all fields from its parent table along with its unique fields.

questions.question: An administrator builds a report on the Task [task] table and sees that it returns records that were created in other tables. Which records can appear because their tables extend Task?

options.text: Lease and Warranty contract records
Incident, Problem, and Change Request records
Application, Computer, and Database CI records
Hardware and Base Configuration Item records

explanation.correct: In the base system, Task is extended by Incident, Problem, and Change Request. Task uses the table per hierarchy model, so the Task table contains all records from its child classes, which is why those records show up in a report built on Task. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/table-administration-and-data-management/table-extension-and-classes.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The docs give Lease [ast_lease] and Warranty [ast_warranty] as tables whose records are replicated in Contract [ast_contract], not as extensions of Task.
Application, Computer, and Database are listed as extensions of the Configuration Item [cmdb_ci] table, not the Task table.
Hardware and Base Configuration Item belong to the CMDB hierarchy (cmdb, cmdb_ci, cmdb_ci_hardware), which is separate from Task.

source.excerpt: Examples of parent tables in ServiceNow include the Task and Configuration Item tables, which are extended to create child classes, like change, request, incident, and problem.

questions.question: An administrator creates a custom table that does not extend any other table, then creates two new tables that extend it. How is the first custom table classified?

options.text: As a child class, since other tables extend it
As a base class, since it extends no other table
As a storage partition of the two new tables
As a child class of the Configuration Item table

explanation.correct: The docs define a table that extends another as a child class and the table it extends as a parent class. A parent class that is not itself an extension of another table is called a base class, so the first custom table is a parent and a base class. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/table-administration-and-data-management/table-extension-and-classes.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A child class is a table that extends another table. Being extended by other tables makes this table a parent class, not a child class.
Partitions are storage tables the system adds under the table per partition model when a database table reaches a storage limit; they are not new extending tables.
The scenario states the custom table extends no other table, so it cannot be a child class of Configuration Item [cmdb_ci].

source.excerpt: Base table serves as a foundation for other tables, but isn't an extension itself.

questions.question: An administrator wants a visual diagram showing which tables reference the Incident table and which tables Incident extends. What should they use?

options.text: A database view that joins Incident and Task
The schema map from Tables & Columns
A dictionary override on the Incident table
A many-to-many definition in sys_m2m

explanation.correct: The schema map displays the details of tables and their relationships visually, including tables that reference, are referenced by, extend, or are extended by the selected table. Generate it from All > System Definition > Tables & Columns by selecting a table and clicking Schema map. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/table-administration-and-data-management/t_GenerateASchemaMap.html and https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/table-administration-and-data-management/c_SchemaMapForTables.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A database view joins two tables virtually to enable reporting on data stored over more than one table. It does not diagram table relationships.
A dictionary override defines a field on an extended table differently from the field on the parent table. It does not show table relationships.
The Many to Many Definitions [sys_m2m] table is used to create custom many-to-many relationships, not to view a diagram of existing ones.

questions.question: An administrator adds a new field to the Incident table in the global application and enters Activity Description as the column label. Which column name does the platform generate by default?

options.text: activity_description
u_activity_description
Activity_Description
u__activity_description

explanation.correct: The column label is the display text shown on list headers and form fields, while the column name is the field name. When a new field is created, the name is generated from the label; for a field in a global application it is prefixed with u_ to mark it as custom, so Activity Description becomes u_activity_description. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/table-administration-and-data-management/r_DictionaryEntryForm.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A name without a prefix is used for a field on a table in the same scoped application; a field in a global application gets the u_ prefix.
Column names can contain only lowercase alphanumeric ASCII characters and underscores, so uppercase letters from the label are not kept.
Consecutive (double) underscores are not allowed in a column name; the platform changes them to a single underscore when the entry is saved.

source.excerpt: Field names are unique and may differ from labels. For instance, city is the field name in the sys_user table for the label Location.

questions.question: An administrator adds a field to a custom task table where users can pick several people from the User table, similar to the Watch list field on Incident. Which field type fits?

options.text: Reference field
Choice list field
Glide list field
Document ID field

explanation.correct: Glide lists allow a user to select multiple records on a table defined by the glide list. The docs give the Watch list field on Incident as the example: it lets the user select records on the User [sys_user] table. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/table-administration-and-data-management/table-relationships.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A reference field allows a user to select a record on the table defined by the field, such as the Caller field selecting a user, not several records.
A choice list lets the user select from a pre-defined set of choices, not records from the User table.
A Document ID field allows a user to select a record on any table in the instance, not multiple records on one table.

source.excerpt: GlideList allows selecting multiple records from a table. Example, Watch List field on the Incident table can link to multiple User table records.

questions.question: A developer creates a conference room booking application in its own application scope. By default, which applications can access and change its tables and business logic?

options.text: Any global application, with no extra configuration
The booking app, unless others are granted access
Global apps, while it can view but not change them
Every app, since it shares the global namespace

explanation.correct: Application scoping protects an application by restricting access to its files and data. In the docs' conference room booking example, the scoped app can access and change its own tables and business logic by default, but other applications cannot unless they are given explicit permission. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/application-development/c_ApplicationScope.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: By default, other application scopes can only read a new scoped app's tables; create, update, and delete access is disabled unless explicitly granted, so global apps cannot change them without extra configuration.
The owning scoped application is not limited to viewing: by default it can access and change its own tables and business logic, and global apps need explicit permission.
Custom applications get a private scope with a unique namespace identifier, so they do not share the global namespace with other apps.

source.excerpt: Scoped apps are sandboxed from the system at large and utilize a restricted API to minimize or prevent damage to anything outside of their scope.

questions.question: An administrator opens a schema map for the Incident table. Which two statements about reading the map are correct? (Choose two)

options.text: The selected table is shown in yellow, usually centered
Relationship types can be shown or hidden with check boxes
Each related table's bar color shows its field data types
The map is a full entity relationship diagram of the tables

explanation.correct: The schema map shows the selected table in yellow, typically centered, with related tables at the sides. The check boxes at the top let you select or clear a relationship type to display or hide tables with that relationship to the selected table. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/table-administration-and-data-management/c_ViewTheSchemaMap.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Each related table has a colored bar indicating its relationship to the selected table (for example, red for Referenced by, green for Extended by), not field data types.
The docs note that because relationships are shown as single lines for simplicity, the diagrams rendered are not entity relationship diagrams.

source.excerpt: Tables with blue bars, including problem and change phase, are tables that extend the task table.

questions.question: An administrator adds a Document ID field named Model ID to a form so users can pick a record from any table. What else does the field need to work?

options.text: A reference qualifier that limits it to a single table
A String table-name field set as its Dependent field
A glide list that stores the selected record sys_ids
A many-to-many definition linking it to each table

explanation.correct: To reference records from any table, two fields work together: one stores the table reference and another stores the record reference. The procedure creates a String field for the table name, then enters that field's column name in the Document ID field's Dependent field. The selected record's sys_id is stored in the Document ID field and the table name in the table reference field. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/t_CreatingADocumentIDField.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Reference qualifiers restrict the records available to reference fields. A Document ID field is meant to reach any table, and needs a table name field instead.
A glide list lets a user select multiple records on one table. The Document ID field itself stores the sys_id of the selected record.
Many-to-many relationships make related records visible from both tables in a related list. They are not part of setting up a Document ID field.

source.excerpt: Document ID fields allows selecting one record from any table. Example, Document field in the Translated Text table.

questions.question: An administrator exports an incident as XML from one instance and imports it into another. Both instances now show the same sys_id for that record. Why?

options.text: The import reused a sys_id freed by a deleted record
A record copied via XML keeps its original sys_id
Sys_ids are derived from the incident's Number value
The new record kept the temporary sys_id of -1

explanation.correct: A unique 32-character GUID called a sys_id identifies each record, and the same sys_id value is never generated twice. Two records share a sys_id only in cases such as a record copied at the database level, or a record copied using an update set or via XML, which keeps the same sys_id. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/c_UniqueRecordIdentifier.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The same sys_id value is never generated twice, so the platform does not reuse sys_ids from deleted records.
A sys_id is a 32-character GUID, not a value built from the record number.
A new record has a sys_id of -1 only until it is inserted, when it is assigned a new sys_id.

questions.question: Lease [ast_lease] extends Contract [ast_contract], which uses the table per class extension model. When a Lease record is created, what happens in Contract?

options.text: Contract stores a replica with the same Sys ID
Contract stores a replica with a new Sys ID
Contract stores nothing; Lease alone has the record
Lease stores nothing; Contract holds the one copy

explanation.correct: In the table per class model, the system creates a separate database table for the parent and each child class. The parent class replicates each record stored in its child classes, and replicated records have the same Sys ID value in each table; the Contract table replicates records from the Lease and Warranty tables. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/table-administration-and-data-management/table-extension-and-classes.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Replicated records have the same Sys ID value in each table, not a new one.
In table per class, the parent class replicates each record stored in its child classes, so Contract does hold a copy.
Storing all records only in the parent table describes table per hierarchy, where child classes have no separate database tables. Table per class gives each child its own table.

questions.question: An administrator needs related records from two tables to appear in a related list on both tables, and also wants to report on two tables joined together. Which two relationship types meet these needs? (Choose two)

options.text: A many-to-many relationship
A database view joining them
A table extension of one table
A Document ID field on one table

explanation.correct: The docs list the ways tables can be related. A many-to-many relationship gives two tables a bi-directional relationship, so related records are visible from both tables in a related list. A database view joins two tables virtually to enable reporting on data stored over more than one table. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/table-administration-and-data-management/table-relationships.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: An extension makes the child table include all fields of the parent and add its own; it does not make related records visible from both tables in a related list or join tables for reporting.
A Document ID field is a one-to-many relationship field that lets a user select a record on any table; it does not provide a bi-directional related list or a reporting join.

questions.question: An administrator imports a user file every week and finds that each run creates duplicate users instead of updating existing ones. What should they configure on the transform map?

options.text: Set Choice action to ignore on each field map
Select Coalesce on a field map with unique values
Select Coalesce empty fields on the email field map
Set Referenced value field name on the email map

explanation.correct: If no coalesce is defined, all imported rows are treated as new records. Selecting Coalesce on a field map makes the import treat that field as a unique key: if an existing target record has a matching value it is updated, otherwise a new record is created. Choose coalesce fields that will have unique values. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/integrate-applications/system-import-sets/c_ImportSetCoalesce.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Choice action only controls what happens when a row contains a reference or choice value that does not exist (create, ignore, or reject). It does not match rows to existing users.
Coalesce empty fields only lets an empty source value match an empty target value. Without Coalesce itself selected, rows are still treated as new records.
Referenced value field name tells the transform how to match incoming values for a reference target field. It does not decide whether a row updates an existing user.

questions.question: On a development instance, an administrator builds a new catalog item with variables while testers submit several orders for it. The update set is then committed to production. What arrives in production?

options.text: The catalog item, its variables, and the submitted orders
The submitted orders, but not the catalog item definition
The catalog item and its variables, but not the orders
The catalog item and the catalog tasks from the test orders

explanation.correct: Update sets capture configuration details but exclude task or process data. The docs use this exact case: an update set records catalog item definitions, variables, and variable choices, but not submitted orders or catalog tasks, so only the configuration reaches production. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/application-development/system-update-sets/customizations-tracked-update-sets.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Submitted orders are process data. Update sets capture configuration such as the catalog item and its variables, not the orders.
This reverses the behavior: the catalog item definition is configuration and is captured, while the submitted orders are not.
Catalog tasks created by the test orders are task data, which update sets exclude; only the item definition and variables are captured.

questions.question: On one instance, a developer creates a custom application in the global scope, and another developer creates a second global application with the same name. What risk does the global scope introduce here?

options.text: Each app gets its own unique namespace prefix
Naming conflicts and data collisions can occur
Both apps become eligible for the ServiceNow Store
Each app's tables are hidden from other global apps

explanation.correct: Global applications do not append a unique namespace identifier to the application name. Because all global applications share the same scope, they bypass scope protections, and the docs warn that creating several global applications with the same name can cause naming conflicts and data collisions. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/application-development/c_GlobalScope.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A unique namespace identifier is what scoped apps get; applications in the global scope do not append a namespace identifier to their name.
Global scope applications can be uploaded to the application repository, but they are not eligible for the ServiceNow Store.
Global applications allow other global applications to read records, run API requests, and create configuration records on their tables.

questions.question: An administrator imports users from a CSV whose Department column holds each department's ID instead of its name. Afterward, users point to new department records named after the IDs. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Referenced value field name was left blank on the map
Coalesce was not selected on the Department field map
Choice action on the Department map was set to reject
Coalesce case sensitive was selected on the user map

explanation.correct: For a reference target field, Referenced value field name specifies which column of the referenced table matches the incoming values. If it is blank, the transform map looks for matches in the display value column; when no match is found, it creates a new record in the reference field's table. Setting it to the column that holds the IDs lets the values match existing records. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/integrate-applications/system-import-sets/t_CreatingAFieldMap.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Coalesce makes a field a unique key for matching import rows to existing target (user) records. It does not control how a reference value is matched to department records.
A reject choice action skips the entire row containing the new value, so it would not create new department records.
Coalesce case sensitive changes how coalesce values match existing target records. It does not affect how reference values are looked up.

questions.question: An administrator is configuring a reference field on a custom table. They want to restrict which records users can select and to control what happens to records that reference a record that is deleted. Which two options apply? (Choose two)

options.text: Reference qualifiers
Cascade delete rules
Reference decorations
Auto-complete settings

explanation.correct: The Reference field type page lists the options for reference fields. Reference qualifiers restrict the records that are available for reference fields, and cascade delete rules specify what should happen to records that reference a record that is deleted. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/c_ReferenceField.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A reference decoration is an icon that appears next to a reference field. It does not restrict records or handle deletions.
Auto-complete controls suggestions as the user types in the field. It does not restrict which records are available or handle deletions.

questions.question: An administrator's user import transform map has the Coalesce checkbox selected on both the email and user_name field maps. When does an import row update an existing user record?

options.text: When a target record matches the row on all coalesce fields
When a target record matches the row on either coalesce field
When Coalesce empty fields is also selected on both maps
When each row supplies the target record's sys_id value

explanation.correct: With multiple-field coalesce, the target record is updated only if it has the same values in all coalesce fields as the staging table record; every coalesce field must match. If no matching record is found, the transform creates a new record instead. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/integrate-applications/system-import-sets/c_ImportSetCoalesce.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Matching on any one of several fields is an OR condition, which needs a conditional coalesce script. Standard multiple-field coalesce requires all fields to match.
Coalesce empty fields only makes an empty value count as a match; it is not required for coalescing on multiple fields.
Returning a sys_id is how conditional coalesce scripts work. Checkbox coalescing compares the coalesce field values, not a sys_id from the row.

questions.question: An administrator wants an Incident field that shows the time between sys_created_on and closed_at, always up to date and without storing the value in the database. Which approach fits?

options.text: A calculated field stored in the database
A function field using glidefunction:datediff()
A Duration field set by a before business rule
A function field using glidefunction:coalesce()

explanation.correct: A function field displays the results of a database query instead of storing data; its value is calculated at retrieval, so it is always up to date. The datediff() operation takes two date/time fields and returns the difference as a duration, for example glidefunction:datediff(closed_at, sys_created_on). See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/platform-support-functions.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The values of calculated fields are stored in the database, which the requirement rules out. Function field values are not stored.
A business rule would store and maintain the result. The docs recommend function fields when logic is a simple transformation of existing fields, without storing the result.
coalesce() returns the first non-empty value from a list of fields; it does not calculate the time between two dates.

questions.question: A service desk agent sees 20 records per page in the Incident list and wants more rows on each page. What can the agent do, and what is the effect?

options.text: Use Show > rows per page; it affects this list alone
Use Show > rows per page; it affects lists they can access
Ask an admin, because this change requires the admin role
Switch list views, since each view sets its own number of rows

explanation.correct: The default is 20 rows per page. Any user can right-click the list title and select Show > <Number> rows per page, and the customized number of rows applies to all lists that the user can access. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-user-interface/configure-use-list-functions.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The docs state that when you customize the number of rows, it applies to all lists that you can access, not just the current list.
No role is required to customize the number of list rows per page.
A view defines which elements appear when a user opens a list. The row count is set with Show > <Number> rows per page.

questions.question: On the Incident table, an administrator directly edits a field that Incident inherits from the parent Task table, without creating a dictionary override. What is the result?

options.text: Only Incident changes; Task is left unaffected
Task and its other child tables change as well
The edit is blocked until it is made on Task itself
Incident gets its own separate copy of the field

explanation.correct: If you edit a field on a child table that is present on the parent table, it is also changed in the parent table and all other child tables. To make a field behave differently on one child table only, use a dictionary override. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/c_IntroductionToFields.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Changing a field on one extended table without affecting the parent or other children requires a dictionary override. A direct edit to an inherited field is also changed in the parent table and all other child tables.
The docs describe the edit taking effect from the child table: it is also changed in the parent table and all other child tables.
Each child class only has Dictionary entries for fields unique to the class; editing an inherited field changes the shared field on the parent and other children.
